questions.problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned} & x+2y+6z=5 \\  & y-10z=-11 \\  & 4x+8y+13z=9\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form.
questions.worked_solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 6 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -10 & -11 \\ 4 & 8 & 13 & 9\end{aligned}].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 6 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -10 & -11 \\ 4 & 8 & 13 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 6 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -10 & -11 \\ 0 & 0 & -11 & -11\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{11}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 6 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -10 & -11 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{aligned}].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
questions.worked_solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & -4 & -20\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned} & x+y+2z=19 \\  & y+2z=13 \\  & z=5,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=5$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y+2(5)=13\,⟹\,y=13-10=3.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=3$ and $z=5$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(3)+2(5)=19\,⟹\,x=6.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=6,y=3$, and $z=5.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨6,3,5⟩.$

questions.problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned} & x+6y-3z=-1 \\  & -2x-12y+8z=1 \\  & -x-5y+4z=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form.
questions.worked_solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ -2 & -12 & 8 & 1 \\ -1 & -5 & 4 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ -2 & -12 & 8 & 1 \\ -1 & -5 & 4 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & -5 & 4 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply the $3$rd row by $\frac{1}{2}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & -6 & 1 & 3 \\ -1 & 4 & -1 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
questions.worked_solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & -6 & 1 & 3 \\ -1 & 4 & -1 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 4 & -1 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-3y=1 \\ y-z=-4 \\ z=1,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=1$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(1)=-4\,⟹\,y=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $y=-3$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-3(-3)=1\,⟹\,x=-8.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=-8$, $y=-3$, and $z=1.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Consider a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix $M\mathbin{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118729/assets/673ea82819858b9a46e0e351a8d6f41b069ed039ee0d31a382110f938f7ef72a.svg)

We can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using the standard Gaussian elimination algorithm. The algorithm that we use is very similar to the case of $2 \times 2$ systems. 

Our goal is to create a descending "staircase" of $1$'s with $0$'s below, and we achieve this using elementary row operations. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & -24\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{6}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix is now in row echelon form, and we can apply back substitution to solve the original system of equations.

**Note:** The row echelon form of a matrix is *not* unique.  In the previous example, after the second row operation we arrived at

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118729/assets/35627a034b30736abb057c01f3251fc047dce780a8cbcf389f8b5c2c2317d766.svg)

This augmented matrix is already in row echelon form! However, it is always useful to do an extra step and obtain $1$'s along the main diagonal, like we did previously:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118729/assets/32a252e05e299a206f2f3776a2a04419f21726e1f8f542cfd4f328dac3251f21.svg)

Having $1$'s along the main diagonal makes the final back substitution process a little easier.

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
Consider a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix $M\mathbin{:}$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118729/assets/673ea82819858b9a46e0e351a8d6f41b069ed039ee0d31a382110f938f7ef72a.svg)

We can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using the standard Gaussian elimination algorithm. The algorithm that we use is very similar to the case of $2 \times 2$ systems. 

Our goal is to create a descending "staircase" of $1$'s with $0$'s below, and we achieve this using elementary row operations. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & -24\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{6}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix is now in row echelon form, and we can apply back substitution to solve the original system of equations.

**Note:** The row echelon form of a matrix is *not* unique.  In the previous example, after the second row operation we arrived at

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118729/assets/35627a034b30736abb057c01f3251fc047dce780a8cbcf389f8b5c2c2317d766.svg)

This augmented matrix is already in row echelon form! However, it is always useful to do an extra step and obtain $1$'s along the main diagonal, like we did previously:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14118729/assets/32a252e05e299a206f2f3776a2a04419f21726e1f8f542cfd4f328dac3251f21.svg)

Having $1$'s along the main diagonal makes the final back substitution process a little easier.

tutorials.name: General Algorithm
tutorials.problem:
The **standard Gaussian elimination** for a $3 \times 3$ system can be described as follows:

- If $a_{11} \neq 0$ and $a_{11} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_1:=R_1/a_{11}.$

- We use first row and the necessary row operations to make the remaining entries of the first column below $a_{11}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{21} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2 + (-a_{21})R_1;$

- if $a_{31} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{31})R_1.$

- If $a_{22} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2/a_{22}.$

- We use the second row and the necessary row operation to make the entry below $a_{22}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{32} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{32})R_2.$

- If $a_{33} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3/a_{33}.$

- In some exceptional cases, such as when the element on the diagonal is equal to $0,$ we first need to exchange rows. Then proceed using the same steps as above.

Carrying out the above algorithm will convert the matrix to row echelon form.
